study_identification.author_journal_year: Coupé et al., Human Brain Mapping, 2022
study_identification.title: Hippocampal-amygdalo-ventricular atrophy score: Alzheimer disease detection using normative and pathological lifespan models

study_characteristics.study_objective: To develop and validate an innovative MRI-based method for Alzheimer disease (AD) detection and mild cognitive impairment (MCI) prognosis using both normative (CN) and pathological (AD) lifespan trajectories. After screening 132 brain structures, the authors propose a novel Hippocampal-Amygdalo-Ventricular Atrophy score (HAVAs) that combines multiple lifespan models to achieve accurate and interpretable classification.

dataset_name.answer: Multi-site aggregated dataset (C-MIND; NDAR; ABIDE; ICBM; IXI; OASIS; ADNI; and 2 other studies [AIBL; MIRIAD for validation])

hc_age.answer: CN subjects ranged from 0.74 years (9 months) to 94 years across all datasets. Dataset-specific ages: C-MIND: mean 8.44 (0.74-18.86); NDAR: mean 12.39 (1.08-49.92); ABIDE: mean 17.53 (6.50-52.20); ICBM: mean 33.75 (18-80); IXI: mean 48.76 (20.0-86.2); OASIS: mean 45.34 (18-94); ADNI: mean 74.81 (60-90)

hc_sex.answer: F 1226 (46.2%), M 1429 (53.8%). Dataset-specific breakdown: C-MIND F129 M107; NDAR F174 M208; ABIDE F84 M408; ICBM F142 M152; IXI F307 M242; OASIS F187 M111; ADNI F203 M201

preprocessing_pipeline.answer: AssemblyNet preprocessing pipeline; image denoising (Manjón et al., 2010); inhomogeneity correction (Tustison et al., 2010); affine registration to MNI space; automatic QC RegQCNet (Denis de Senneville et al., 2020); second inhomogeneity correction in MNI space (Ashburner & Friston, 2005); intensity standardization (Manjón & Coupé, 2016); segmentation using 250 DL models based on Neuromorphometrics protocol (132 structures)

quality_checking_detail.answer: Automatic QC using RegQCNet (Denis de Senneville et al., 2020). For all training subjects detected as failure by automatic QC, a visual assessment was performed by individually checking the input images and the segmentations using a 3D viewer. Subjects confirmed as failures by the expert were removed from the training dataset. Number of excluded subjects not explicitly reported.

site_effect_handling_detail.answer: No explicit site effect handling method was described in the paper. Volume normalization by ICV and z-score normalization were used to compensate for inter-subject and inter-structure variabilities, but no specific batch correction or site effect modeling was mentioned.

modeling_method.answer: Polynomial lifespan models; z-score normalization to ICV; HAVAs computation based on distance to both CN and AD models

software_tool.answer: AssemblyNet; custom HAVAs code (will be available via volBrain platform and AssemblyNet-AD)

response_variable.answer: Brain volumes: hippocampus; amygdala; inferior lateral ventricle; and HAVAs (combined score = hippocampus + amygdala - inferior lateral ventricle). All volumes expressed as z-scores of normalized volumes (percentage of ICV).

predictor_effects.answer: Age is modeled as a fixed effect using polynomial models (linear, quadratic, or cubic). No random effects are specified. Model selection based on F-statistic (ANOVA), T-statistic for coefficients (p<.05), and Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC).

nm_vldtn_handle_ns.reason: Volume normalization by ICV and z-score normalization address inter-subject and inter-structure variability. However, no explicit handling of site/scanner effects, age nonlinearity is addressed through polynomial models (quadratic/cubic). Sex is not included as a predictor. No discussion of heteroscedasticity, correlation structure, or other nuisance factors.
nm_vldtn_handle_ns.supporting_text: To compensate for the inter-subject variability, we normalized all the structure volumes using the intracranial cavity volume (ICV). Moreover, in order to be able to combine several structures with different sizes, we performed z-score normalization of all the normalized volumes. ... We considered several low order polynomial models: Linear model, Quadratic model, Cubic model.
nm_vldtn_handle_ns.location: Section 2.3 Volume normalization; Section 2.4 Lifespan model estimation

nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.reason: No same-domain non-independent validation (e.g., cross-validation, train-test split within the same dataset) is reported for the normative model.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.supporting_text: No explicit mention of cross-validation or internal validation on the training dataset.

nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.reason: The training dataset (ADNI, C-MIND, NDAR, ABIDE, ICBM, IXI, OASIS) was used to build the models, and external datasets (AIBL, MIRIAD) were used for testing. No independent hold-out validation within the same domain (training datasets) is described.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.supporting_text: Training used 7 datasets (C-MIND; NDAR; ABIDE; ICBM; IXI; OASIS; ADNI). Validation used external datasets AIBL and MIRIAD.

nm_vldtn_diff_domain.reason: External validation was performed on completely unseen datasets (AIBL and MIRIAD for diagnosis; ADNI sMCI/pMCI for prognosis), demonstrating generalization to different domains. Additionally, a sensitivity analysis swapped training and testing datasets (AIBL, OASIS, MIRIAD for training; ADNI for testing).
nm_vldtn_diff_domain.supporting_text: To validate our model, we built a testing dataset based on two open access databases (AIBL and MIRIAD) to perform AD versus CN diagnosis task. Therefore, we validated the generalization capacity of our method and its robustness to domain shift. ... Finally, in order to test the consistency of our findings, we changed training and testing datasets: AIBL, OASIS, and MIRIAD databases were used for training and ADNI was used for testing.
nm_vldtn_diff_domain.location: Section 2.1.2 Testing dataset; Section 2.1.3 Sensitivity analysis; Section 3.5

clinical_dataset.answer: AIBL for AD; MIRIAD for AD; ADNI for sMCI and pMCI

diseases_studied.answer: Alzheimer's Disease (AD); Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) - stable MCI (sMCI) and progressive MCI (pMCI)

clinical_groups_n.answer: AD: 128 (AIBL: 82, MIRIAD: 46); sMCI: 255; pMCI: 235. Training AD patients: 377 (OASIS: 45, ADNI: 332)

clinical_groups_age.answer: Training AD: OASIS mean 77.04 (63-96), ADNI mean 75.13 (55-91). Validation: AIBL AD mean 74.8 (55.5-93.4); MIRIAD AD mean 69.3 (55.6-85.8); ADNI sMCI mean 72.3 (55-89.5); ADNI pMCI mean 74.0 (55-88.0)

clinical_groups_sex.answer: Training AD: OASIS F29 M16 (F64.4% M35.6%); ADNI F151 M181 (F45.5% M54.5%). Validation: AIBL AD F47 M36 (F56.6% M43.4%); MIRIAD AD F27 M19 (F58.7% M41.3%); ADNI sMCI F100 M155 (F39.2% M60.8%); ADNI pMCI F103 M132 (F43.8% M56.2%)

deviation_metric.answer: HAVAs score: probability of being AD patient based on distance to both CN and AD lifespan trajectories. Score computed using cumulative distribution function of standard normal distribution weighted by the distance between CN and AD models (δ = |volCN(Age) - volAD(Age)|). Classification threshold: 50% (equal distance between both models).

clinical_application_and_analysis.association_analysis: Classification performance evaluated using balanced accuracy (BACC), specificity (SPE), sensitivity (SEN), and area under the curve (AUC). Comparison with normative modeling (2σ threshold), classical machine learning methods (SVM with RBF kernel, LASSO logistic regression), and state-of-the-art deep learning methods (ROI-based CNN, subject-based CNN, patch-based CNN from Wen et al., 2020).
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_brief: HAVAs achieved very accurate AD detection (AUC ≥94% on external datasets AIBL and MIRIAD) and accurate discrimination between progressive MCI and stable MCI (AUC=78% on ADNI), outperforming normative modeling, classical ML, and recent DL methods while maintaining interpretability.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_detailed: HAVAs demonstrated superior classification performance compared to single-structure models and state-of-the-art methods. For diagnosis (AD vs CN): AIBL achieved BACC=88%, AUC=94%; MIRIAD achieved BACC=89%, AUC=96%. For prognosis (sMCI vs pMCI): ADNI achieved BACC=73%, AUC=78%. HAVAs outperformed the second-best method (ROI-based CNN) by 3 percentage points for both diagnosis and prognosis. Among individual structures, amygdala provided the best performance, followed by hippocampus and inferior lateral ventricle. The combination of these three structures (HAVAs) consistently outperformed any single structure across all methods tested (multimodel, normative modeling, SVM, LASSO). Normative modeling using only hippocampus obtained the worst results (16 percentage points lower than HAVAs). Sensitivity analysis with swapped training/testing datasets (AIBL, OASIS, MIRIAD for training; ADNI for testing) produced similar results (BACC=87%, AUC=93%), confirming robustness to training domain selection and good generalization capability.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_limitations: The paper does not explicitly describe limitations in a dedicated section. Potential limitations inferred from the methodology include: (1) No explicit handling of site/scanner effects despite using multi-site data; (2) Sex is not included as a predictor variable in the lifespan models; (3) Polynomial models may not capture complex non-linear age trajectories; (4) The AD lifespan model relies on mixing AD patients (55-96y) with young CN subjects (<55y), assuming slow progressive neurodegeneration; (5) Limited sample size for some datasets (e.g., MIRIAD CN N=23); (6) No discussion of potential confounders such as comorbidities, medication, or genetic factors.
clinical_application_and_analysis.application_notes: HAVAs offers several advantages over recent deep learning approaches: (1) Conceptual simplicity and full interpretability based on distance to AD or CN trajectories, making it well-suited for clinical practice or pharmaceutical trials; (2) Very low number of parameters (<10 per trajectory) compared to CNNs (>10 million parameters), enabling better generalization and robustness to domain shift; (3) No hyperparameters needed for combining structures thanks to volume normalization procedure; (4) Fast implementation and easy to re-implement. Software will be made freely available as a downloadable Docker (https://github.com/volBrain/AssemblyNetAD) and as an online pipeline on the volBrain platform (http://www.volbrain.net/). The screening of 132 structures, 5 lobes, 4 regional tissues, and 3 tissues identified 33 brain areas showing significant divergence between AD and CN models, with amygdala, hippocampus, and inferior lateral ventricle being the most discriminant.

general_notes.general_notes: This study introduces an innovative dual-model approach (normative CN + pathological AD lifespan models) that bridges the gap between normative modeling and classification-based methods. The AD lifespan model was constructed by mixing 377 AD patients (55-96y) with 1,874 young CN subjects (<55y), based on the assumption that neurodegeneration is a slow and progressive process. The paper provides extensive comparison with multiple baselines including normative modeling, classical ML (SVM, LASSO), and state-of-the-art DL methods (Wen et al., 2020). Model selection for polynomial trajectories was based on F-statistic (p<.05), T-statistic for all coefficients (p<.05), and Bayesian Information Criterion. Most selected models were quadratic except for inferior lateral ventricle (cubic). The study used ClinicaDL software to define groups in AIBL and ADNI, ensuring consistent selection criteria with prior work. Alternative combination strategies were tested: hippocampal-ventricle ratio (HVR) showed 7% point BACC drop; adding temporal lobe reduced BACC by 1% point; using weights for combining structures provided marginal improvement (<1-2% points). Authors chose unweighted combination for simplicity. Training dataset: N=3,032 (2,655 CN; 377 AD). Validation dataset: N=1,039 (490 CN, 128 AD, 255 sMCI, 235 pMCI). Full dataset list recorded: C-MIND (236 CN), NDAR (382 CN), ABIDE (492 CN), ICBM (294 CN), IXI (549 CN), OASIS (298 CN, 45 AD), ADNI (404 CN, 332 AD for training; 255 sMCI, 235 pMCI for validation), AIBL (467 CN, 82 AD), MIRIAD (23 CN, 46 AD).
